subject: botany
question_text: Give the economic importance of plants belonging to Fabaceae.

verification.note: Chapter 8 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section (book pp.21-22), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star rank and NO year citation — so `stars` is 0 and `appearances` is empty by construction, not by omission. Only ONE botany source book is held: there is no TSBIE Basic Learning Material for botany (the copy in hand is physics-only) and no botany board paper in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the back-test against a real paper are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this chapter. This card is NOT-CHECKED — do not read that as checked-and-clean. The mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. BOOK WORDING: the book lists "Red grams, black grams, green grams", "Indian rose wood" and "menthi". Botanical names are used here in their place; "menthi" is fenugreek, Trigonella foenum-graecum. Fodder is given as Phaseolus in the book; clover and lucerne are added as the standard fodder legumes.

steps.label: Pulses and oils
lines: Pulses, whose seeds are rich in protein:
steps.why: Fabaceae seeds are rich in protein, so pulses are the first use any examiner expects.
common_mistakes: Giving only common names. Add the botanical name for at least one plant in each group.
Listing cereals. Cereals are Poaceae, not Fabaceae.
steps.memory_tip: Six uses, six headings: pulses, oils, timber, fibre, vegetables, fodder. Then add the extras.
steps.margin_note: Head each use, then give two named examples. Do not write paragraphs.

steps.label: Timber and fibre
lines: sun hemp (Crotalaria juncea) gives a strong bast
steps.why: Fabaceae includes large trees as well as herbs, which is why one family can supply both a pulse and a timber.
common_mistakes: Naming teak. Teak is Verbenaceae or Lamiaceae, not Fabaceae.
Naming cotton as the fibre. Cotton is Malvaceae.
steps.memory_tip: Two hard woods and one soft fibre: red sanders, rosewood, sun hemp.
steps.margin_note: Two named timbers and one fibre plant fill this mark.

steps.label: Vegetables and fodder
lines: (Medicago sativa) are grown to feed cattle.
steps.why: The same protein-rich seed that feeds people also feeds cattle, so vegetables and fodder are two sides of one property.
common_mistakes: Confusing fodder with green manure. Fodder is eaten; green manure is ploughed in.
steps.memory_tip: Pea, beans and fenugreek are eaten; clover and lucerne are fed to cattle.
steps.margin_note: Two or three named vegetables plus one fodder plant.

steps.label: Other uses
lines: Root nodules fix nitrogen, so Crotalaria and
Sesbania are ploughed in as green manure.
steps.why: Nitrogen fixation is the property that makes the whole family important to farming, so it belongs in any full answer.
common_mistakes: Leaving out nitrogen fixation, which is the family’s biggest contribution.
Writing that the nodules make nitrogen. The bacteria in them fix nitrogen from the air.
steps.memory_tip: Food for people, fodder for cattle, and nitrogen for the soil.
steps.margin_note: One extra line on nitrogen fixation lifts a plain list into a full answer.

insider_note: This is a list question, so the marks come from the number of NAMED uses. Six headings with examples beat two headings written well.
